newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS-Tough road ahead for Ukraine's budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tough road ahead for Ukraine's budget.

text.p: Ukraine unveiled a tough 1997 draft budget on Friday calling for wide-ranging spending cuts and tax reforms which Western diplomats said would require strong arm-twisting from the top to win approval in parliament.

"The president (Leonid Kuchma) and prime minister (Pavlo Lazarenko) will have to go to bat for it," one Western diplomat said. "Ever since independence the economy has slid down, down and down, and this is the only way out."
The revised draft budget, submitted to parliament on Friday, foresees lower payments to pensioners and war veterans, and puts a stop to free public transport and rent subsidies.
It even touches the most sacred cow of all, with plans to halve payments to the fund for victims of the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster which takes up 12 percent of budget spending.
"We must re-define the social welfare system in this country, and discussions will no doubt be turbulent," said Deputy Finance Minister Stanyslav Bukovynsky.
Parliament, which will begin reviewing and debating the draft next week, is dominated by left-leaning deputies who favour Soviet-style benefits and subsidies to citizens.
"The majority of deputy groups and fractions (parties) will not vote in favour of this revised budget," said Reform party leader Serhiy Sobolev, Interfax news agency reported.
Ukrainians, worn down by difficult economic conditions, are also not expected to welcome the measures.
Another Western diplomat said the budget will be a measure of how serious Kuchma is about economic reform.

"This will require a Constitution-scale effort to get this budget through," he said, referring to the dramatic all-night session in June when the president pushed through the country's first post-Soviet constitution.
"Parliament is never consistent in what it wants," he added.

The draft, agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), forecasts a budget deficit of 5.8 billion hryvnia ($3.1 billion), or 5.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- four percent by Western calculations.
It proposes revenue of 37 billion hryvnia and expenditure of 42.8 billion hryvnia.
"The draft budget is based on support for the industrial producer, and lowering taxes," Lazarenko told parliament.

Sticking to tight monetary policy would also pave the way for Ukraine to receive a three-year, $2.5 to $3.0 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) from the IMF next year to succeed the $867 million stand-by programme negotiated in May.
The IMF board, which would not approve the EFF until next month or early next year, has already given outline approval to the economic reform plans.
The constitution states that the budget must be passed by January 1, although Ukraine has always missed the deadline in previous years.
Consisting of 90 documents, the budget also promised to deliver badly-needed tax reform to broaden the tax base and relieve heavy tax burdens on businesses.
It promised to begin a system of unemployment benefits in 1997 but government officials did not state when they would be able to pay a $1.5 billion wage bill owed to government workers.
The budget forecast annual inflation at 25 percent, down from an expected 40 percent this year and 181 percent in 1995.

It gave no forecast for economic growth in 1997, though an earlier draft in October predicted the country's first economic growth since independence -- 1.7 percent, after contraction of 11.8 percent last year.
($1 = 1.871 hryvnia)
